passages.p1:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit in two parallel rows of four persons each. Row 1 persons face south and Row 2 persons face north, so every person in Row 1 faces exactly one person in Row 2.
A faces E. F sits immediate right of A. B faces H. C sits at an extreme end of Row 1. D sits second to the left of E. B sits at an extreme end of a row, but not in the same row as A.
passages.p2:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P live on seven different floors of a building, numbered 1 (ground) to 7 (topmost). Each owns a car of a different colour: red, blue, white, black, grey, green and silver.
There are exactly two floors between J and L. N lives on a floor above J and below L. O lives immediately above K. M lives below K but above J. P lives immediately above J. K owns the blue car and J owns the black car. The person on the top floor owns the silver car and the person on the fifth floor owns the grey car. The owner of the red car lives below K. The person living immediately below L owns the green car. L does not own the white car.
passages.p3:
Five friends P, Q, R, S and T are a doctor, an engineer, a lawyer, a teacher and a pilot, not necessarily in that order. Each lives in a different city among Delhi, Pune, Goa, Agra and Surat.
Q is neither the doctor nor the teacher. R is neither the pilot nor the doctor. S is the teacher. The pilot lives in Surat and the lawyer lives in Delhi. The doctor lives neither in Delhi nor in Goa. S lives neither in Goa nor in Pune. Q lives in Goa. P does not live in Surat.

questions.text:
What should come in place of the question mark?

2, 5, 12, 27, 58, ?
questions.explanation: Each term is the previous term × 2 plus n, with n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: 58 × 2 + 5 = 121.
questions.trap: Doubling without the rising addend.

questions.text:
Select the option that will come next in the series.

ACF, DGK, HKP, MOU, ?
questions.explanation: Treat the three positions separately. First letters: A, D, H, M move +3, +4, +5, so the next is +6: S. Second letters: C, G, K, O move +4 each, so next is S. Third letters: F, K, P, U move +5 each, so next is Z.
steps: First letters A, D, H, M: gaps 3, 4, 5, then 6: M + 6 = S
Second letters C, G, K, O: gap 4: O + 4 = S
Third letters F, K, P, U: gap 5: U + 5 = Z
Cluster: SSZ
questions.trap: Assuming all three positions follow the same rule.
questions.revise: Letter-cluster series with different rules per position
questions.shortcut: Write the three letter columns separately and find each gap.

questions.text:
Select the number that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number.

17 : 304 :: 12 : ?
steps: 15 = 17 − 2, so the rule is n² + n − 2
questions.trap: Stopping at n(n + 1) and missing the − 2.
wrongReasons: Used n² + n and forgot to subtract 2

questions.text:
Select the option that is related to the third term in the same way as the second term is related to the first term.

BAD : 14 :: FOG : ?
steps: 7 × 2 = 14, so double the sum
questions.trap: Giving only the sum and missing the doubling.
wrongReasons: Added the letter values but did not double

questions.text: Pointing to a woman, Kiran said, 'Her husband is the only son of my mother's mother.' How is the woman related to Kiran?
questions.explanation: Kiran's mother's mother is his maternal grandmother. Her only son is Kiran's maternal uncle. The woman is that uncle's wife.
steps: Mother's mother = maternal grandmother
Her only son = Kiran's maternal uncle
The woman is his wife: wife of maternal uncle
questions.trap: Mixing up the mother's side and the father's side.
wrongReasons: She is married into the family, not born into it
The grandmother is the mother of her husband, not the wife
The relative is on the mother's side
questions.approach: Resolve the phrase from the inside out: mother's mother, then her son, then his wife.

questions.text:
In a certain code, 'A + B' means 'A is the mother of B', 'A − B' means 'A is the brother of B', 'A × B' means 'A is the father of B' and 'A ÷ B' means 'A is the sister of B'.

If P × Q ÷ R + S, how is P related to S?
questions.explanation: P × Q: P is the father of Q. Q ÷ R: Q is the sister of R, so P is also the father of R. R + S: R is the mother of S. P is the father of S's mother, so P is S's maternal grandfather.
steps: P × Q: P is Q's father
Q ÷ R: Q and R are siblings, so P is R's father too
R + S: R is S's mother
P is the father of S's mother: maternal grandfather
questions.trap: Choosing paternal because the symbol chain looks male-line.
wrongReasons: R, who is S's mother, is P's daughter, so P is on the mother's side
P is two generations above S
P is a generation higher than an uncle
questions.shortcut: Translate each symbol, then decide on whose side the link to the child runs.

questions.text: In a row of students, Anil is 12th from the left and Bina is 15th from the right. If they exchange their positions, Anil becomes 25th from the left. How many students are there in the row?
questions.explanation: After the exchange Anil stands where Bina stood, so Bina was 25th from the left. She is also 15th from the right. Total = 25 + 15 − 1 = 39.
steps: Anil's new place = Bina's old place
Bina: 25th from left, 15th from right
questions.trap: Using Anil's old rank of 12, which is a distraction.
questions.revise: Rank from both ends after an exchange
wrongReasons: Added 25 and 15 without removing the shared place
Added Anil's original rank (12) and Bina's rank (15)
questions.shortcut: Total = rank from left + rank from right − 1 for the same person.

questions.text:
Statements:
Some tables are chairs.
All chairs are sofas.
No sofa is a bed.

Conclusions:
I. Some sofas are tables.
II. No chair is a bed.
III. All tables are sofas.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: Some tables are chairs and all chairs are sofas, so some tables are sofas, and the converse gives I. Chairs are sofas and no sofa is a bed, so no chair is a bed: II. Only some tables are chairs, so we cannot say all tables are sofas: III fails.
steps: Tables ∩ chairs, chairs ⊂ sofas: some tables are sofas, so some sofas are tables (I)
Chairs ⊂ sofas and sofas have no beds: no chair is a bed (II)
'Some' tables cannot be stretched to 'all': III fails
questions.trap: Extending 'some' to 'all' in the last conclusion.
wrongReasons: II also follows: chairs are sofas and no sofa is a bed
III fails: only some tables are chairs
questions.approach: Draw tables and chairs overlapping, chairs inside sofas, and beds fully outside sofas.

questions.text:
In the following question, the symbols are used as: 'P @ Q' means P > Q, 'P # Q' means P < Q, 'P $ Q' means P = Q, 'P % Q' means P ≥ Q and 'P & Q' means P ≤ Q.

Statement: P # Q & R @ S $ T

Conclusions:
I. P < R
II. R > T
III. Q > S

Which of the conclusions definitely follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: The statement reads P < Q ≤ R > S = T. P < Q ≤ R gives P < R (I). R > S = T gives R > T (II). Q and S are both below R but their relation is not given, so III is not certain.
steps: Decode: P < Q ≤ R > S = T
P < Q ≤ R: P < R, so I follows
R > S = T: R > T, so II follows
Q and S are both smaller than or equal to R only: III is uncertain
questions.trap: Linking two items that share only a larger common element.
wrongReasons: II also follows: R > S = T
I also follows, and III does not
questions.shortcut: In a chain with a peak (≤ then >), items on opposite sides of the peak cannot be compared.

Option A (Figure A) is out: Mangoes sits outside fruits, which is false.
Option B (Figure B) is out: Mangoes and sweet things are swapped.
Option D (Figure D) is out: Fruits, mangoes and sweet things are drawn as separate sets.
Common slip to avoid: Drawing sweet things as separate from mangoes.
So the answer is option C: Figure C.
questions.trap: Drawing sweet things as separate from mangoes.
wrongReasons: Mangoes sits outside fruits, which is false

questions.text:
Who is the tallest among P, Q, R, S and T?

I. Q is taller than R and S; R is taller than T, and T is taller than P.
II. S is taller than P.
options: Neither statement is sufficient even together
questions.explanation: From I: Q > R > T > P and Q > S, so Q is taller than all four others. II only compares S and P, which does not help, and cannot settle the tallest on its own.
steps: I: Q > R > T > P and Q > S, so Q is tallest
II: S > P only, so the tallest is still unknown
I alone is sufficient
questions.trap: Feeling that both statements must be used.
wrongReasons: II only says S is taller than P
II adds nothing to what I already settles
I alone already makes Q the tallest
questions.approach: Test each statement on its own before combining.

questions.text: If '+' means '×', '−' means '÷', '×' means '−' and '÷' means '+', then find the value of 36 − 9 × 4 + 3 ÷ 5.
questions.explanation: Replace the symbols: 36 ÷ 9 − 4 × 3 + 5. By BODMAS: 36 ÷ 9 = 4, 4 × 3 = 12, so 4 − 12 + 5 = −3.
steps: Expression: 36 ÷ 9 − 4 × 3 + 5
questions.trap: Calculating with the printed signs or left to right.
wrongReasons: Worked from left to right ignoring BODMAS
Treated the last operation as subtraction

questions.text: In a class of 60 students, 35 play cricket, 28 play football and 10 play neither game. How many students play both games?
questions.explanation: Students playing at least one game = 60 − 10 = 50. Both = 35 + 28 − 50 = 13.
steps: At least one game: 60 − 10 = 50
Cricket + football = 35 + 28 = 63
questions.trap: Forgetting to remove those who play neither.
wrongReasons: Subtracted 60 and forgot the 10 who play neither
That is the number who play only football
That is the number who play only cricket

questions.text: How many pairs of letters in the word PLANTED have as many letters between them in the word as there are between them in the English alphabet (counting in either direction)?
questions.explanation: Pairs: P and T have three letters between them in the word (L, A, N) and three between them in the alphabet (Q, R, S). L and N have A between them in the word and M in the alphabet. E and D are adjacent in the word and adjacent in the alphabet. That makes 3.
steps: Positions: P1 L2 A3 N4 T5 E6 D7
P (16) and T (20): 4 apart in both
L (12) and N (14), positions 2 and 4: 2 apart in both
E (5) and D (4), positions 6 and 7: 1 apart in both
Total 3
questions.trap: Counting only pairs that appear in alphabetical order.
wrongReasons: Counted only pairs in forward alphabetical order
Counted an extra pair with unequal gaps
questions.shortcut: Compare the position gap with the alphabet-value gap for each pair.

questions.text: How many triangles are there in the following figure?
questions.explanation: Eight lines meet at the apex, so any two of them with the base form a triangle: C(8,2) = 28.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Triangles = C(k,2) for k lines from the apex.
Option B (7) is out: Only the smallest triangles counted.
Option C (21) is out: One line fewer assumed.
Option D (36) is out: One extra line assumed.
Common slip to avoid: Counting only the 5 small triangles.
So the answer is option A: 28.
questions.trap: Counting only the 5 small triangles.
questions.revise: Triangles = C(k,2) for k lines from the apex

questions.text: Two positions of the same cube are shown. Which number is on the face opposite to 4?

questions.explanation: Between the two views the cube is turned about the vertical axis with 6 on top. Face 4 has turned out of view and the face now at the left (5) came from behind it, so 5 is opposite 4.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite.
Option A (2) is out: 2 is next to 4 in the first view.
Option B (6) is out: 6 is on top in both views, next to 4.
Option C (1) is out: 1 is never visible, so it cannot be fixed by these views.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 2, which is next to 4 in the first view.
So the answer is option D: 5.
questions.trap: Choosing 2, which is next to 4 in the first view.
questions.revise: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite
wrongReasons: 2 is next to 4 in the first view
6 is on top in both views, next to 4
1 is never visible, so it cannot be fixed by these views
